title: What Hath God Wrought
subtitle: The electric telegraph from patent office to newspaper: Washington, Baltimore, London, Slough and Munich, 1837–1845
intro: In 1837 three electric telegraphs appeared within months of one another. In London, William Fothergill Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented a needle instrument in June. In Munich, Carl August Steinheil showed the Bavarian Academy a line that printed dots on paper tape in July. In New York, Samuel Morse, a painter turned professor, gave his first public demonstration in September and filed a caveat at the Patent Office that autumn. None of the three was yet news. The chapter follows how, over the next eight years, the wire stopped being a lecture-room curiosity and began to carry things people cared about: votes, nominations, and in January 1845 a description of a man wanted for murder.

The American story is unusually well documented because it ran through Congress. Committee reports, the House vote of February 1843 and Morse's report of June 1844 to the Treasury are government records. Morse's letters to his brother Sidney, printed by his son in 1914, show the same months from inside: the waiting, the money running out, the quarrels on the construction gangs. Alfred Vail, who sat at the Baltimore end of the line, and Ezra Cornell, who built it, appear in their agreements, patents and later papers. Little of this is diary in the strict sense. The record is mostly dated letters, official reports, newspaper columns and court testimony, and the form tags say so.

The heart of the chapter is the line between the Capitol in Washington and the Baltimore and Ohio depot in Baltimore in May 1844. On 1 May, before the line was finished, Vail sent the Whig ticket from Annapolis Junction about an hour ahead of the train. On 24 May came the message chosen by Annie Ellsworth, the young daughter of the Commissioner of Patents. Five days later the Democratic convention in Baltimore nominated Silas Wright, who was in the Senate in Washington, for vice-president. He declined by wire, and the delegates did not believe a machine could have brought his answer.

In Britain the telegraph grew along the railways. Cooke and Wheatstone's line ran beside the Great Western from Paddington, and by 1843 it reached Slough. On the evening of 1 January 1845 a woman named Sarah Hart was found dying at Salt Hill near Slough. A description of the man seen leaving her house was telegraphed to Paddington ahead of his train. John Tawell was followed, arrested the next morning, tried at Aylesbury and hanged in March. The case is told here soberly, through the police and court record and the press. It made the telegraph famous in a way no demonstration had.

Behind both stories runs a quarrel over credit. Joseph Henry at Princeton had shown in 1831 how to drive an electromagnet through a long wire, and he advised and endorsed Morse. When Vail's 1845 book left him out, the rift began. It ended in Morse's printed attack of 1855 and a Smithsonian Regents' report clearing Henry. In Britain, Cooke and Wheatstone went to arbitration in 1841 over who had invented what. These disputes are set out as positions with their evidence. The book takes no side.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Clock times are local as the sources give them. Washington and Baltimore kept local solar time, and the Slough message gives the train's departure as 7.42 p.m. by railway time. Some letters were dated by their writers and others reconstructed by editors, and the entries say which. Several famous scenes, including Annie Ellsworth's visit on 4 March 1843 and Cornell's account of halting the pipe-laying, survive only in later recollections. They are marked approx.

eyes.name: Samuel Finley Breese Morse
eyes.role: Painter and professor of the literature of the arts of design at the University of the City of New York, aged 46 in 1837; superintendent of the government test line in 1843–44
eyes.side: United States; holder of the Morse patent with Vail, Gale and F. O. J. Smith
eyes.where: New York; then Washington, at the Capitol terminal of the line
eyes.vantage_label: the patentee at the Washington key
eyes.authenticity: His letters are in the Samuel F. B. Morse Papers, Library of Congress (about 6,500 items). A large selection was edited by his son Edward Lind Morse as Samuel F. B. Morse: His Letters and Journals (1914), which sometimes supplies dates and runs passages together. The 1843 House tally differs between two of his letters (89–80 and 89–83). His reports to the Treasury are printed as congressional documents.
eyes.bio: Morse came to electricity from painting and lost a commission for the Capitol Rotunda in 1837, the same year he went public with his telegraph. His letters to his brother Sidney are a running account of a man staking everything on one appropriation. His public reports read as calm and confident. The letters underneath are anxious, pious and often angry.

sources.title: Samuel F. B. Morse, His Letters and Journals, vol. II (1914), Project Gutenberg
Library of Congress, Samuel F. B. Morse Papers: Invention of the Telegraph
House Doc. No. 270, 28th Congress, 1st Session (June 1844)

eyes.name: Alfred Lewis Vail
eyes.role: Machinist and former theology student from the Speedwell Iron Works family, Morristown, New Jersey; Morse's partner from 1837 and assistant on the government line at three dollars a day
eyes.where: Annapolis Junction (1 May 1844), then the Baltimore and Ohio depot in Baltimore
eyes.vantage_label: the operator at the Baltimore end
eyes.form: dated letters, agreements, a published book (1845)
eyes.authenticity: His papers, including research notebooks, journals and correspondence with Morse, are at the Smithsonian Institution Archives (Record Unit 7055), with more at the New Jersey Historical Society. His book The American Electro Magnetic Telegraph appeared in 1845. Whether he, rather than Morse, devised the dot-and-dash alphabet is still argued.
eyes.bio: Vail put up money and workshop skill and built the instruments. He sat at the far end of every famous transmission and sent the answers back. He got little of the credit and the code that bears Morse's name may be partly his. He has a strong claim to be the first full-time telegraph operator in America.

sources.title: Smithsonian Institution Archives, A Forgotten History: Alfred Vail and Samuel Morse
Morse, Letters and Journals vol. II (agreement of 21 March 1843; letters to Vail)

eyes.name: Ezra Cornell
eyes.role: Self-taught mechanic and plough salesman from Ithaca, New York, aged 36 in 1843; hired to lay and then string the Washington–Baltimore line
eyes.where: Maine (summer 1843), then along the Baltimore and Ohio right of way
eyes.authenticity: His patent of 28 February 1844 survives with its drawing. His papers are at Cornell University Library. Much of the colourful construction story, including the claim that he deliberately broke his trenching plough to stop the failing pipe work without embarrassing Morse, comes from his own later accounts and his son's biography. Those parts are recollection, not record.
eyes.bio: Cornell came into the story by building a machine that dug a trench and laid pipe in one pass. Then he watched the buried line fail. His reading in the Patent Office library that winter led him to argue for wires on poles. He later made his fortune in Western Union and founded the university that bears his name.

sources.title: Cornell University Library exhibit: The Telegraph (1843–1844)
Cornell Chronicle, The Ezra Files: Getting involved with the telegraph

eyes.name: Joseph Henry
eyes.role: Professor of natural philosophy at the College of New Jersey (Princeton), aged 40 in 1837; first Secretary of the Smithsonian from 1846
eyes.where: Princeton; London in spring 1837; Washington from 1846
eyes.vantage_label: the scientist whose principles it ran on
eyes.form: dated letters, sworn deposition, published statements
eyes.authenticity: His correspondence and notebooks are edited in The Papers of Joseph Henry (Smithsonian). His letter to Morse of 24 February 1842 was printed in House Report No. 17 of December 1842. His 1849 deposition and the Regents' 1857 proceedings on Morse's charges are printed records.
eyes.bio: Henry showed in 1831 that a high-resistance 'intensity' magnet could be worked through a long wire. He built a classroom telegraph and later a relay, and he never patented any of it. He advised Morse and backed his bid to Congress. Then he found himself written out of Vail's book and attacked by Morse in print. His side of the quarrel is a scientist's protest against being treated as a mere predecessor.

sources.title: David Hochfelder, Joseph Henry: Inventor of the Telegraph? (Smithsonian)
Smithsonian Institution Archives, Telegraphs, Controversy, and the Board of Regents

eyes.name: Silas Wright Jr.
eyes.role: Democratic senator from New York, aged 49, close ally of Martin Van Buren
eyes.where: Washington, a few rooms from Morse's terminal in the Capitol
eyes.vantage_label: the nominee who said no by wire
eyes.form: telegraphed replies and a dated letter (as reported)
eyes.authenticity: The exact wording of his telegraphed refusals does not survive in the sources consulted here. His written declination was carried to Baltimore by hand and read to the convention. Accounts of the exchange come from Morse's report, convention proceedings and later histories, and they differ on detail and timing.
eyes.bio: Wright was nominated for vice-president because the convention had just passed over his friend Van Buren for James K. Polk. Loyal to Van Buren, he refused at once. The refusal reached the delegates by wire. They had nominated him less than two hours earlier and doubted it was real.

sources.title: Jacksonian America: The 1844 Democratic National Convention
Morse, Letters and Journals vol. II, May 1844

eyes.name: Charles Goadsby Ferris
eyes.role: Democratic congressman from New York, reporting for the House Committee on Commerce
eyes.vantage_label: the committee man who wrote the bill
eyes.authenticity: House Report No. 17, 27th Congress, 3rd Session, dated 30 December 1842, with appendices including Henry's letter of February 1842 and Morse's letter of 6 December 1842. A US government record.
eyes.bio: Ferris's report made the case to the House that the telegraph was a question of national defence and commerce, and possibly a rival to the Post Office. It asked for the $30,000 test line that passed ten weeks later. It also set out the European competition, naming Wheatstone and Steinheil.

sources.title: House Report No. 17, 27th Cong., 3rd Sess. (30 Dec 1842)

eyes.name: Willie Person Mangum
eyes.role: Whig senator from North Carolina and president pro tempore of the Senate in 1844
eyes.authenticity: His papers are published in an edited edition. The phrase cited here is quoted by the US Senate Historical Office; the exact date of the letter is not given there.
eyes.bio: Mangum was a political opponent of the Democrats meeting in Baltimore. He was also one of the Washington politicians who crowded round Morse's instrument for news of their rivals' convention. His reaction shows how quickly the wire became a political tool, used by both sides.

sources.title: US Senate, Morse's Telegraph in the Capitol

eyes.name: The Baltimore Patriot and its Washington correspondent
eyes.vantage_label: the first paper to print news by wire
eyes.authenticity: The paper's 25 May 1844 report of a House vote on the Oregon question is listed as the first telegraphed news dispatch in Kane's Famous First Facts. The wording of the dispatch is not reproduced here because it was not seen in a primary copy.
eyes.bio: Newspapers had depended on express riders and the mails. On the day after the 24 May message, a Washington correspondent sent the paper the result of a House vote over the wire. The press, more than Congress, would turn out to be the telegraph's best customer.

sources.title: House Divided project (Dickinson College), first telegraphed news bulletin

eyes.name: Carl August von Steinheil
eyes.role: Professor of mathematics and physics at Munich and member of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences, aged 36 in 1837
eyes.where: Munich: the Academy, the observatory at Bogenhausen and his house in Lerchenstraße
eyes.authenticity: Steinheil described his system in his own publications of 1838. The summary here relies on Hugo Marggraff's article in Die Gartenlaube (1887), transcribed on German Wikisource. It is a later, admiring account, and its priority claims against Morse are partisan.
eyes.bio: Steinheil's Munich line linked three stations by wires over rooftops and on masts and printed raised and lowered dots on a moving strip. In 1838 he found that the earth itself could carry the return current, which halved the wire. Morse's 1842 report to Congress named him as a rival.

sources.title: H. Marggraff, C. A. Steinheil und der erste Schreibtelegraph, Die Gartenlaube 1887 (Wikisource)

eyes.name: William Fothergill Cooke
eyes.role: Former Indian Army officer and anatomical modeller, aged 30 in 1836; business partner and promoter of the Cooke and Wheatstone telegraph
eyes.where: Heidelberg (1836), London, then the Great Western line from Paddington
eyes.vantage_label: the promoter who put it on the railways
eyes.form: dated letters to his mother; pamphlets
eyes.authenticity: His letters, mostly to his mother, are in the Cooke Papers at the IET Archives (SC MSS 007). Latimer Clark edited Extracts from the Private Letters of the Late Sir W. F. Cooke (1895). His later pamphlets against Wheatstone are partisan.
eyes.bio: Cooke saw a needle telegraph demonstrated in a lecture at Heidelberg and went home to sell the idea to the railways. He needed a scientist and found Wheatstone. He also needed money and kept his family informed of every hope, which is why his letters survive. The quarrel over credit with Wheatstone shadowed both men for the rest of their lives.

sources.title: Science Museum Group Journal, A tale of two telegraphs
IET Archives, Cooke Papers, Volume I of personal correspondence

eyes.name: Charles Wheatstone
eyes.role: Professor of experimental philosophy at King's College London, aged 35 in 1837
eyes.authenticity: His papers are at King's College London. The record used here is public: joint patents, his evidence to the 1840 Select Committee on Railway Communication, the 1841 arbitration and his 1855 Reply to Mr Cooke's Pamphlet. He left no diary of these years.
eyes.bio: Wheatstone supplied the science of the partnership and had his own long lines of wire under King's College. In 1837 he met Joseph Henry, who described his relay to him. The press tended to give him sole credit for the Great Western telegraph, which infuriated Cooke.

sources.title: Science Museum Group Journal, A tale of two telegraphs
King's College London, Wheatstone exhibition: Murder and the telegraph

eyes.name: William Williams
eyes.role: Sergeant of the Great Western Railway police at Paddington
eyes.where: Paddington station, then the City of London
eyes.vantage_label: the policeman who met the train
eyes.authenticity: His evidence was reported in the press accounts of the Aylesbury trial, March 1845. The summary here relies on the British Transport Police history page, which draws on those reports.
eyes.bio: Williams was the man the telegraph message was written for. He was in plain clothes at Paddington, picked out the passenger described and followed him across London. Tawell mistook him for an omnibus conductor and handed him the fare. The arrest the next morning made a railway policeman part of the first famous wire-assisted manhunt.

sources.title: British Transport Police, The murder of Sarah Hart

eyes.name: The Times (London)
eyes.authenticity: The Times reported the Great Western telegraph in 1840 and the Tawell arrest, trial and execution in 1845. The issues are not cited here by date because they were not seen directly. The quoted phrase is taken from the University of Salford history page.
eyes.bio: The Times turned a local crime into a national lesson about the wire. Its coverage gave the telegraph more publicity than any demonstration. Its readiness to credit Wheatstone alone for the Great Western line was part of what drove the partners to arbitration.

sources.title: University of Salford, John Tawell

entries.headline: A lecture-room needle telegraph sets Cooke going
entries.digest: At Heidelberg, Cooke watched Professor Georg Wilhelm Muncke illustrate a lecture with a needle telegraph built on Pavel Schilling's principle. He had come to study anatomical modelling. Within weeks he was building instruments of his own and planning to sell the idea to the new railways.
entries.source_note: Science Museum Group Journal; Cooke's own letters (IET SC MSS 007). The exact day, often given as 6 March, was not confirmed.

entries.headline: Cooke tells his mother Wheatstone is ahead of him
entries.digest: Writing to his mother, Cooke reports that Wheatstone is the one man close to what he is attempting. Wheatstone already has miles of wire ready and two or three telegraphs. The letter marks Cooke's shift from rival to partner.
entries.quote: the only man near the mark
entries.source_note: Letter of 27 Feb 1837, cited in Science Museum Group Journal, 'A tale of two telegraphs', n. 11

entries.headline: Henry shows Wheatstone how a relay could work
entries.digest: On his European tour, Joseph Henry met Wheatstone in London and described the relay arrangement he had worked out at Princeton about 1835. Henry later counted this meeting as proof that the principles of the telegraph were common scientific property before anyone patented them.
entries.source_note: D. Hochfelder, 'Joseph Henry: Inventor of the Telegraph?' (Smithsonian). Month not pinned.

entries.headline: The first British electric telegraph patent
entries.digest: Cooke and Wheatstone were granted a joint patent for giving signals and sounding alarms at a distance by electric currents. It was the first English patent for an electric telegraph. The instrument was the five-needle board, on which two needles swung together to point at a letter.
entries.source_note: ETHW gives 12 June 1837, other sources 10 June; Science Museum Group Journal (patent No. 7390)

entries.headline: Steinheil's writing telegraph shown to the Academy
entries.digest: Steinheil demonstrated his apparatus to the Bavarian Academy of Sciences. Double wires, partly strung over rooftops and masts, linked the Academy, the Bogenhausen observatory nearly 5 km away and his own house. Ink-fed points printed upper and lower dots on a moving paper strip, at most four dots to a character.
entries.source_note: H. Marggraff, Die Gartenlaube 1887, no. 37, pp. 605–606 (Wikisource)

entries.place: Euston to Camden Town, London and Birmingham Railway
entries.headline: A trial along the London and Birmingham line
entries.digest: Cooke and Wheatstone ran a trial line from Euston to Camden Town for the London and Birmingham Railway. Wheatstone sat at one end and Cooke at the other. The railway was impressed but would not pay for it, and its engineers kept their rope-haulage signals. The five-wire cost was a burden.
entries.source_note: Science Museum Group Journal (year only); the day is the date usually cited. ETHW dates a first message on this line to 4 Sept 1837.

entries.place: University of the City of New York
entries.headline: Morse demonstrates his recording telegraph
entries.digest: Morse showed his telegraph in public at the university, sending signals through a long coil of wire to a pencil that marked a moving strip. Watching was Alfred Vail, who within weeks had signed on as a partner with his family's ironworks behind him.
entries.source_note: Hochfelder (Smithsonian) gives 2 Sept; ETHW gives 4 Sept 1837

entries.headline: A caveat to guard the American claim
entries.digest: Alarmed by news of European telegraphs, Morse filed a caveat with the Patent Office describing his American Electro-Magnetic Telegraph. This was a notice of an invention still being perfected. The full patent followed in June 1840. The caveat became his main exhibit whenever priority was disputed.
entries.source_note: Morse, Letters and Journals vol. II, ch. XXIV (Oct 1837–May 1838); the day (often 6 Oct) was not confirmed

entries.place: House Committee on Commerce room, Capitol
entries.headline: A demonstration for President Van Buren
entries.digest: Morse set up his instrument in the Commerce Committee room for members of Congress, President Martin Van Buren and his cabinet. The committee chairman, F. O. J. Smith of Maine, recommended $30,000 for a fifty-mile test line. Smith then became a partner in the patent. The bill died in the Panic of 1837.
entries.source_note: US Senate Historical Office, 'Morse's Telegraph in the Capitol'

entries.headline: The earth can carry the return current
entries.digest: Testing whether railway rails could serve as conductors, Steinheil found that current passed through the moist ground between them. Buried metal plates at each end could therefore replace the second wire. He used the method on his Munich line.
entries.source_note: Marggraff, Die Gartenlaube 1887 (Wikisource)

entries.place: Paddington to West Drayton, Great Western Railway
entries.headline: The first commercial line opens beside the Great Western
entries.digest: Cooke's line from Paddington to West Drayton, about thirteen miles, went into service beside the Great Western Railway. It used four-needle instruments, with the wires first laid in iron pipe. It was the first electric telegraph in regular commercial use.
entries.source_note: London Museum, 'How the telegraph took off in Victorian London' (1839); opening day commonly given as 9 July

entries.headline: The Times credits Wheatstone alone
entries.digest: The Times described the telegraph at work on the Great Western as Wheatstone's. The article largely concerned his dial instrument. Cooke saw it as part of a pattern of the press naming the professor and forgetting the man who built the lines.
entries.source_note: Cited in Science Museum Group Journal, 'A bittersweet victory'

entries.headline: Brunel and Daniell settle who invented what
entries.digest: After about five months, the arbitrators, Isambard Kingdom Brunel for Cooke and John Frederic Daniell for Wheatstone, issued their award. It credited Cooke with making the telegraph a practical working undertaking and Wheatstone with the scientific research that made it possible. Neither man was satisfied for long.
entries.source_note: Science Museum Group Journal, 'A bittersweet victory'; wording of the award summarised from standard accounts, not seen directly

entries.headline: Henry backs Morse over Wheatstone and Steinheil
entries.digest: Replying to Morse, Henry wrote that of the electromagnetic telegraphs he knew, he preferred Morse's. Morse put the letter in front of Congress, and it was printed in the House report of December 1842. It became an awkward document years later, when Henry insisted he had only endorsed the instrument, not its originality.
entries.quote: I should prefer the one invented by yourself
entries.source_note: House Report No. 17 (1842), appendix A; Morse, Letters and Journals vol. II

entries.headline: The Commerce Committee asks for $30,000
entries.digest: Ferris reported for the Committee on Commerce that the usefulness of telegraphs was settled and that Morse's should be adopted for defence and commerce. The report reviewed Steinheil's needle system in Bavaria and Wheatstone's in Britain. It printed Morse's alphabet and asked for $30,000 for a test line under his superintendence.
entries.source_note: House Report No. 17, 27th Cong., 3rd Sess.

entries.headline: Waiting on the House
entries.digest: Morse wrote to Sidney that the bill had still not been reached. He told the family to prepare for failure. His money was nearly gone, and he was rehearsing how to bear defeat as God's will.
entries.source_note: Morse, Letters and Journals vol. II, letter to Sidney E. Morse

entries.headline: Mesmerism amendment laughed down
entries.digest: The bill came out of committee of the whole after a mocking amendment was rejected. It proposed giving half the money to experiments in mesmerism. Morse told Sidney the clouds were starting to break.
entries.quote: the clouds begin to break away
entries.source_note: Morse to Sidney, 21 Feb 1843; Congressional Globe, Morse, Letters and Journals vol. II

entries.headline: The House passes the bill by six votes
entries.digest: Morse reported to Sidney that the House had passed the bill, giving the tally as 89 to 80. In a letter to Smith he gave 89 to 83, the figure usually cited. Many members did not vote. Opponents, among them Cave Johnson of Tennessee, had treated it as a joke.
entries.quote: passed the House by a vote of 89 to 80
entries.source_note: Morse to Sidney, 23 Feb 1843 (Library of Congress, Morse Papers bound volume June 1842–Sept 1843); Letters and Journals vol. II

entries.headline: The Senate passes it on the last night
entries.digest: Morse wrote to Smith that the Senate had passed the bill without division and without opposition. He sent Vail a jubilant note the same day. He had gone home believing it would fail in the end-of-session crush and seems not to have known that the President had signed it at midnight.
entries.quote: passed my bill without division and without opposition
entries.source_note: Morse to F. O. J. Smith and to Vail, dated 3 March 1843, Letters and Journals vol. II; Act of 3 March 1843 cited in House Doc. 270

entries.headline: Annie Ellsworth brings the news and is promised the first message
entries.digest: As Morse told it later, Annie Ellsworth, the daughter of the Commissioner of Patents, met him at breakfast to congratulate him. Her father had seen the President sign the bill. Morse promised her she should choose the first message on the finished line.
entries.quote: I have come to congratulate you
entries.source_note: Morse's later letter to Bishop Stevens, printed in Letters and Journals vol. II

entries.headline: Vail signs on at three dollars a day
entries.digest: Vail agreed to serve as Morse's assistant on the government line at three dollars a day. He was a part-owner of the patent and was now also a salaried employee on the project his money had kept alive.
entries.source_note: Agreement printed in Morse, Letters and Journals vol. II

entries.headline: A plough that digs and lays pipe at once
entries.digest: In the office of F. O. J. Smith, Cornell found Smith struggling with a design for laying the telegraph's lead pipe. At Smith's request he built a plough that cut the trench, laid the pipe and covered it in one pass. Morse came to see it and hired him.
entries.source_note: Cornell University Library exhibit, 'The Telegraph (1843–1844)'

entries.headline: Trenching begins, and the insulation fails
entries.digest: The pipe-laying began on the railway line. Cornell soon suspected that the wire insulation had been damaged when the pipe was made and warned Morse, who halted the work. Miles of pipe had to be dug up or abandoned. Cornell's later account that he broke the plough on purpose is recollection only.
entries.source_note: Morse, Letters and Journals vol. II; Cornell Chronicle, 'The Ezra Files'

entries.headline: Fisher dismissed, Cornell hired
entries.digest: In his report to the Treasury, Morse said he had dismissed his assistant Dr Fisher for neglect. He had taken on Ezra Cornell at $1,000 a year as an efficient mechanical assistant. His private letters that month described a project falling apart amid quarrels with Smith and the contractors.
entries.source_note: Morse to Secretary of the Treasury, 27 Dec 1843, Letters and Journals vol. II

entries.headline: Only Vail stays loyal
entries.digest: Morse told Sidney that Fisher and Gale were gone and that Smith had turned hostile. Of the original circle, only Vail was still at his post. He was weighing whether to start again on poles.
entries.quote: Vail only remains true at his post
entries.source_note: Morse to Sidney, 13 Jan 1844, Letters and Journals vol. II

entries.headline: Cornell patents his trench machine
entries.digest: Cornell received a patent for a machine for cutting trenches and laying pipes. By then the buried line had been given up. Over the winter, reading in the Patent Office and congressional libraries, he had concluded that overhead wire on insulated poles was the only practical way.
entries.source_note: Patent certificate and drawing, Cornell University Library exhibit

entries.headline: Six miles of wire on poles
entries.digest: Morse reported that six miles of line on poles were working and that posts had been set as far as Beltsville. After the winter's failures he wrote that his fortunes were turning.
entries.quote: A brighter day is dawning upon me
entries.source_note: Morse to Sidney, 10 April 1844, Letters and Journals vol. II

entries.headline: The Whig ticket by wire, an hour ahead of the train
entries.digest: With the line finished only to Annapolis Junction, Vail took news from a passing train that the Whigs in Baltimore had nominated Henry Clay, with Theodore Frelinghuysen for vice-president. He sent it to Morse at the Capitol, where it was received about an hour before the train reached Washington. Doubters took it for a lucky guess until the train confirmed it.
entries.source_note: US Senate Historical Office; Morse to Sidney, 7 May 1844

entries.headline: Morse describes the Frelinghuysen message
entries.digest: Morse wrote to Sidney about the Whig news received the week before. He timed one exchange over the unfinished line at two minutes and one second. He was preparing to finish the line to Baltimore within days.
entries.quote: in two minutes and one second
entries.source_note: Morse to Sidney, 7 May 1844, Letters and Journals vol. II

entries.headline: Annie Ellsworth's text goes down the line
entries.digest: Before a small invited company in the Capitol, Morse sent the words Annie Ellsworth had chosen, with her mother's help, from Numbers 23:23. Vail took them down in Baltimore and sent them straight back. The ceremony was private. The real test came in the busy days that followed.
entries.source_note: Library of Congress, paper tape of 24 May 1844 (Morse Papers); Letters and Journals vol. II

entries.headline: Vail receives and returns the message
entries.digest: At the Baltimore depot, Vail's register embossed the dots and dashes on paper tape. He read the message without error and sent the same words back to Washington. Morse's own report of 3 June gives the Baltimore terminal as the railroad depot on Pratt Street.
entries.source_note: Library of Congress tape; House Doc. 270 (Pratt Street depot)

entries.headline: The first news column by wire
entries.digest: The Washington correspondent of the Baltimore Patriot sent the paper the result of a House vote on the Oregon question over the new line. It is usually counted as the first news report carried by electric telegraph. Within days other papers were printing telegraphic paragraphs.
entries.source_note: Kane, Famous First Facts, p. 635, via House Divided project (Dickinson College)

entries.headline: Vail sends Washington the Polk nomination
entries.digest: Vail relayed the ballots from Baltimore as messengers brought them from the convention hall. On the ninth ballot, James K. Polk was nominated. Morse later reported that the news reached Washington and came back to Baltimore before the presiding officer had announced it.
entries.source_note: House Doc. 270 (Morse's report, 3 June 1844); Jacksonian America

entries.headline: Wright declines the vice-presidency by wire
entries.digest: Told by telegraph that the convention had nominated him for vice-president, Wright refused at once by the same wire. He refused a second time when pressed. The delegates doubted the message and sent men to Washington to check, and Wright sent a letter declining in writing.
entries.source_note: Jacksonian America; Calvert, 'The Electromagnetic Telegraph' (dates the nomination 27 May, other accounts 29 May)

entries.headline: A Whig senator watches the Democrats by wire
entries.digest: Mangum, the Senate's president pro tempore and an opponent of the convention's party, joined the crowd at Morse's room for the Baltimore news. He called the result a miraculous triumph of science. Politicians of both parties were learning to follow their rivals in near real time.
entries.source_note: US Senate Historical Office, 'Morse's Telegraph in the Capitol'; letter date not given there

entries.headline: The refusal confirmed; Dallas nominated
entries.digest: Wright's written refusal was read to the convention, which accepted that the telegraph had told the truth. After two more ballots the delegates nominated George M. Dallas of Pennsylvania instead.
entries.source_note: Jacksonian America, 'The 1844 Democratic National Convention'

entries.headline: Crowds at the window, and a fear of pride
entries.digest: Morse told Sidney that a crowd of some hundreds had called him to the window of the Capitol during the convention days. He called Annie Ellsworth's sentence divinely indited and worried that the public praise might make him proud. He noted that Cave Johnson, who had mocked the bill, had changed his mind.
entries.source_note: Morse to Sidney, 31 May 1844, Letters and Journals vol. II; US Senate Historical Office

entries.headline: Report to the Treasury: the experiment has succeeded
entries.digest: Morse reported that the forty-mile line from the Capitol to the Pratt Street depot was complete and its practicability fully established. He cited the convention traffic, a family's fears about a death in Baltimore settled in ten minutes, and a bank inquiry answered at once. Posts had proved better than pipe, and about $3,500 was left. He offered the line to the government.
entries.source_note: House Doc. No. 270, 28th Cong., 1st Sess. (received 6 June 1844)

entries.headline: Wheatstone sells out to Cooke
entries.digest: Wheatstone accepted a single payment of £30,000 for his share of the joint patents, leaving Cooke in full control. In September the Electric Telegraph Company was advertised in The Times. The settlement ended the business partnership but not the argument over credit.
entries.source_note: Science Museum Group Journal

entries.headline: The press credits the wire
entries.digest: Reporting the arrest, The Times said the capture would have failed without the telegraph at Slough and Paddington. The case made the Great Western line, until then a curiosity charging the public to send messages, suddenly famous.
entries.quote: Had it not been for the efficient aid of the electric telegraph
entries.source_note: Quoted by University of Salford, 'John Tawell'; the issue date was not confirmed

entries.headline: A wired description meets the 7.42 from Slough
entries.digest: After Sarah Hart was found dying at Salt Hill, the stationmaster at Slough had a description of the man seen leaving her house telegraphed to Paddington. The man wore Quaker dress and had taken the 7.42 p.m. train. Sergeant Williams met the train, picked out the passenger and followed him by omnibus into the City. The passenger took him for the conductor and paid him the fare. Williams kept him in sight to his lodging without arresting him.
entries.source_note: British Transport Police, 'The murder of Sarah Hart'; University of Salford, 'John Tawell'

entries.place: Jerusalem Coffee House, Cornhill, City of London
entries.headline: Tawell arrested the next morning
entries.digest: Williams, with Inspector Wiggins of the Metropolitan Police, arrested John Tawell at the Jerusalem Coffee House. Tawell was a former convict transported to Australia who had returned a wealthy man and lived as a Quaker. He denied having been at Slough.
entries.source_note: British Transport Police history page

entries.headline: Waiting again on Congress
entries.digest: Morse wrote to his daughter that he was in an unpleasant suspense over the bill to extend the line and keep it running. Congress voted only $8,000 to keep the Washington–Baltimore line going for a year under the Post Office. Several senators asked what the telegraph was actually for.
entries.quote: I am now in a state of unpleasant suspense
entries.source_note: Morse to Mrs Lind, 8 Feb 1845, Letters and Journals vol. II; US Senate Historical Office (1845 appropriation)

entries.headline: Williams gives evidence at the trial
entries.digest: Tawell's trial opened at Aylesbury before Baron Parke, with Fitzroy Kelly for the defence. Williams described meeting the train and following the prisoner. The medical evidence was that Sarah Hart had died of poisoning, which the defence tried to explain away. The jury convicted.
entries.source_note: British Transport Police history page; day of Williams's testimony not confirmed

entries.headline: Execution reported
entries.digest: Tawell was hanged outside the court at Aylesbury at 8 a.m. before a crowd put at about ten thousand. The press coverage of the case gave as much attention to the telegraph that caught him as to the crime.
entries.source_note: British Transport Police history page; King's College London, 'Murder and the telegraph'

entries.headline: Morse sees Wheatstone's system at Rugby
entries.digest: Touring Europe to sell his patent, Morse inspected Wheatstone's needle telegraph at Rugby. He wrote to Vail that a machine which recorded messages had an incalculable advantage over one whose needles had to be watched. Weeks later he wrote from Paris that the French had not adopted Wheatstone's system either.
entries.quote: The advantage of recording is incalculable
entries.source_note: Morse to Vail, 1 Sept 1845, Letters and Journals vol. II

entries.headline: Vail's book leaves Henry out
entries.digest: Vail published The American Electro Magnetic Telegraph, a detailed account of Morse's system and the government line. It gave almost no credit to Joseph Henry. Henry took the omission as the first public sign that the Morse camp meant to treat his work as irrelevant.
entries.source_note: Hochfelder (Smithsonian): 'Fall 1845'

entries.headline: Henry testifies against Morse's broad claims
entries.digest: Subpoenaed in telegraph patent litigation, Henry gave a deposition setting out his own discoveries and stating that he knew of no original discovery in electricity by Morse. Morse took it as a betrayal. The Smithsonian Regents later called the deposition correct in all its historical details.
entries.source_note: Hochfelder (Smithsonian): subpoenaed 1849–52; Calvert cites the 'no original discovery' testimony in Smith v. Downing (1850); Regents' wording from Smithsonian Archives blog

entries.headline: Morse's 'Defence' attacks Henry
entries.digest: Morse published a long Defence against Henry's deposition in a telegraph trade magazine. It ran to more than ninety pages and questioned Henry's honesty as well as his science. Henry asked the Smithsonian Regents to investigate.
entries.source_note: Hochfelder (Smithsonian); Smithsonian Archives blog

entries.headline: The Regents take up Morse's charges
entries.digest: Henry laid Morse's article before the Board of Regents, who appointed a committee to examine it. Their report found the charges not just unproved but disproved. Historians now generally see Henry as the source of the principles and Morse as the man who made a working system and a business.
entries.quote: not only remain unproved but they are positively disproved
entries.source_note: Smithsonian Institution Archives, 'Telegraphs, Controversy, and the Board of Regents'; date of committee report not confirmed

claims.claim: Munich Academy ↔ Bogenhausen observatory ↔ Lerchenstraße: test signals printed as dots on paper strip over a roughly 5 km rooftop line
Commerce Committee room, Capitol: demonstration messages for President Van Buren and cabinet; committee then recommends $30,000
Priority position (Britain): Brunel–Daniell award credits Cooke with the practical undertaking, Wheatstone with the science; both later dispute it in pamphlets (1854–57)
Henry (Princeton) → Morse: endorses Morse's telegraph over Wheatstone's and Steinheil's; letter laid before Congress
House passes the $30,000 telegraph bill 89–83 (Morse to Sidney first gives 89–80); many members not voting
claims.evidence: Morse letters of Feb 1843 (Library of Congress; Letters and Journals vol. II)

claims.claim: Senate passes the bill without division on the last night; President signs at midnight; Annie Ellsworth brings Morse the news next morning (later recollection)
claims.evidence: Morse to Smith, 3 Mar 1843; Morse to Bishop Stevens (later); Act of 3 Mar 1843

claims.claim: Vail at Annapolis Junction → Morse at Capitol: Whig ticket Clay and Frelinghuysen; received about an hour before the train
claims.evidence: US Senate Historical Office; Morse to Sidney, 7 May 1844

claims.claim: Morse, Supreme Court chamber, Capitol → Vail, Baltimore depot, and back: "What hath God wrought" (Numbers 23:23, chosen by Annie Ellsworth)
claims.evidence: Library of Congress paper tape, Morse Papers

claims.claim: Washington correspondent → Baltimore Patriot: result of a House vote on the Oregon question, the first wired news dispatch
claims.evidence: Kane, Famous First Facts p. 635, via House Divided

claims.claim: Baltimore → Washington → Baltimore: Polk's nomination reaches Congress and returns to the convention before the official announcement
Wright in Washington → convention in Baltimore: declines the vice-presidential nomination by wire, twice; delegates doubt it until his letter arrives; Dallas nominated 30 May
Slough station → Paddington: a murder at Salt Hill; suspect in Quaker dress (spelt KWAKER, the instrument having no Q) on the 7.42 p.m. train, first-class ticket; Paddington asked for a repeat
claims.evidence: University of Salford, 'John Tawell'; British Transport Police

claims.claim: Paddington and Metropolitan police: Tawell arrested at the Jerusalem Coffee House after being followed overnight
Morse (London) → Vail: has seen Wheatstone's needle system at Rugby; recording gives his own the advantage
Priority position (US): Henry's 1849 deposition; Morse's Defence (Jan 1855); Smithsonian Regents find Morse's charges disproved (1857); Hochfelder: Henry supplied principles, Morse a working system

convergences.label: Three telegraphs in one year
convergences.note: London patented needles in June, Munich printed dots in July, and New York marked a strip in September. Henry had already told Wheatstone how a relay could work. Each group later read the others' dates as a threat.

convergences.label: The appropriation passes
convergences.note: Ferris's report made the case in December. The House passed the bill by six votes and the Senate without a division. Morse went to bed expecting failure, and Vail got the news in a two-line note.

convergences.label: The Whig ticket beats the train
convergences.note: On a line still under construction, the first useful message was political news. Vail sent it, Morse received it and Cornell's crew had just strung the wire it came over.

convergences.label: What hath God wrought
convergences.note: The famous message was a private, ceremonial exchange. The next day's newspaper dispatch was the first sign of what the line would actually be used for.

convergences.label: The convention by wire
convergences.note: For the first time a party convention was followed in near real time by the men it was choosing and by their opponents. Wright was the first politician to turn down an office by telegraph, and the first to be disbelieved because of it.

convergences.label: The Slough message
convergences.note: A railway telegraph built to signal trains caught a fugitive on one. The policeman acted on the message and the press spread the story. Cooke's company gained the publicity it had never managed to buy.

convergences.label: Morse at Rugby
convergences.note: The American rival inspected the British system and reported to Vail that his own recording register was better. Meanwhile Wheatstone was selling out to Cooke.

convergences.label: The credit quarrels harden
convergences.note: Vail's book and the Cooke–Wheatstone settlement came in the same season. On both sides of the Atlantic the question of who invented the telegraph moved from letters into print and courts.

ties.note: Vail saw Morse's 1837 demonstration and became his partner; he sat at the far end of the 1844 line.
Morse hired Cornell in 1843 to lay the pipe and kept him on at $1,000 a year to build the line on poles.
Henry advised and endorsed Morse from 1839 to 1842; from 1845 they were bitter opponents over credit.
Henry described his relay to Wheatstone in London in 1837.
Partners from May 1837, then rivals through arbitration (1841), a buy-out (1845) and pamphlets (1850s).
Ferris's committee printed Henry's 1842 letter as an appendix to its report.
The 1842 House report named Steinheil's Bavarian system as a European competitor.
Wright's refusals and Vail's convention bulletins passed each other on the same wire on 29 May 1844.
A Whig and a Democratic senator in the same building, both following the Democratic convention by wire.
Williams acted on a message sent over the Great Western line Cooke had built and extended to Slough.
The Times credited Wheatstone with the Great Western telegraph in 1840, one of the slights behind the arbitration.
Wheatstone opposed Morse's English patent application in 1838. Morse inspected his system at Rugby in 1845.
The Patriot's correspondent used Morse's line the day after the inaugural message.

threads_out.note: Morse's 1842 renewed push in Congress was spurred partly by news of a French proposal for an optical telegraph system. The new electric lines grew up in direct competition with semaphore networks of the Chappe type.

In August 1843 Morse told the Treasury that a telegraph could certainly be laid across the Atlantic, and he had tested an underwater cable in New York harbour in October 1842. Fifteen years later he was an adviser to the Atlantic Telegraph Company.
Joseph Henry, the scientist behind the electromagnet and relay in this chapter, was the Smithsonian Secretary whom Alexander Graham Bell consulted in March 1875 while working on the telephone.
Cooke and Wheatstone's telegraph was built for and alongside the new railways, first the London and Birmingham, then the Great Western. The Washington–Baltimore line ran along the Baltimore and Ohio.

The Washington–Baltimore line was the start of a network that, by the 1860s, let Lincoln read generals' dispatches in the War Department telegraph office. Cornell's Western Union completed the transcontinental line in October 1861.
